transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. I came in because, well, I barely sleep right anymore. I'll just lie in bed hearing rain, or thinking about the bluff giving way. And then when I finally do pass out, I end up waking up all sweaty from these dreams. It's just getting to be too much, because I show up to my shifts at the call center feeling like I never even went to sleep.
When you're lying in bed hearing the rain or thinking about the bluff, are you able to eventually fall asleep, or do you find yourself staying awake most of the night?

I mostly stay awake for hours. Like I said, I do eventually pass out, but it takes a really long time. I just lie there stuck listening for the rain, or picturing the bluff giving way again. And then when I finally do manage to get to sleep, it's just ruined by those dreams where I wake up covered in sweat. 

So, yeah, I guess I get some sleep eventually, but it doesn't really count for much. I still show up to the call center feeling like I never even closed my eyes.
You mentioned thinking about the bluff giving way — when did that incident happen, and did your sleep problems start around the same time?

Yeah, they started right around the same time. The incident happened about four months ago. The trail on the bluff collapsed, and... well, I got trapped. So, yeah, this whole thing with my sleep has been going on for about four months, basically ever since that day.

You mentioned the incident happened about four months ago and your sleep problems started around the same time. Just to be clear — have you been having these sleep problems continuously for all four months since the bluff collapsed, or did they start a bit later after the incident?
Yeah, it's been pretty much continuous. It started right after it happened, and it's been going on for the whole four months since I got trapped on the trail.

When you're thinking about the bluff giving way during the day or when you're awake, does it feel like you're actually experiencing the event happening again, or is it more like you're just remembering what happened?

It's... it's more like it's actually happening again. Stuff just pops into my head out of nowhere. Like, I'll hear the sound of rocks sliding, or I'll feel like my leg is stuck under me again. And for a minute, I'm right back on that trail, instead of just sitting at my desk with my headset on. It feels real.

When you feel like you're back on that trail—like when you hear the rocks sliding or feel your leg stuck—do you know at that moment that you're actually at your desk at the call center, or do you completely lose track of where you really are?

Well, it's... I guess for a minute I completely lose track of where I am. Like I said, stuff just pops into my head out of nowhere. I'll hear those rocks sliding or feel my leg trapped, and it's like I'm right back on that trail. For that second, I'm not at my desk or wearing my headset... I'm just back there. It takes me a minute to snap out of it and realize I'm actually at work.
When you snap out of it and realize you're at work, how do you know you're back at your desk? Like, what helps you realize it's not actually happening?

I'm not really sure, honestly. I don't think there's any specific thing that helps me realize it. I guess I just... blink and look around, and the feeling just kind of fades away. I just eventually notice I'm sitting in my chair and not out there anymore.

When you're back on that trail during these moments—when you hear the rocks sliding or feel your leg trapped—are you able to still see and hear things around you at the call center, or is it like the present completely disappears and you're only aware of being on the trail?

I mean, when it happens, the call center just kind of... goes away. I don't hear the phones ringing or see my computer screen or anything. It's just... the rocks and the dirt and being stuck. It's like the present completely disappears for that second until I snap back to it.

During these moments when you're back on the trail and the call center disappears—when you snap back to reality, can you remember what happened during that time, or is there a blank spot in your memory?

I remember it. There's no blank spot or anything like that. I know exactly what I was seeing and feeling in my head when I was back on the trail. I just don't remember what was happening around me in the office during that time, because I wasn't really... there, I guess. But I remember the flashback itself clearly.
